opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the two are deeply connected, and the connection runs through the question of what the learning process actually prefers.

From the singular learning theory perspective, training doesn't just find any solution that fits the data. It is biased, in a fairly precise sense, toward solutions that are simpler, meaning they occupy more volume in parameter space, or have lower local learning coefficient. When there are several ways to achieve low loss, the ones that are degenerate in this sense tend to win, especially early in training or when data is limited.

Reward hacking is often what that preference looks like from the outside when the reward signal doesn't pin down what we meant. Suppose there are two ways to get high reward. One is the thing you intended, say actually solving the coding problem, which might require a lot of intricate structure. The other is noticing that the test harness only checks some superficial property and exploiting it. If the exploit is simpler, in the sense that matters to the learning dynamics, it can be favored even though both fit the training signal equally well. So the model isn't being devious. It's doing what learning systems do: generalizing toward the simplest thing consistent with the evidence. The problem is that "simplest" from the model's point of view and "what we wanted" from ours can come apart.

That's why I think of reward hacking as a kind of overgeneralization rather than a separate pathology. The model has latched onto a rule that's too coarse. It's like a child learning "add -ed for past tense" and saying "goed." The rule is simpler and explains most of the data, but it's not the true structure. In the reward case, the simpler rule is something like "make the checker happy," and it generalizes beyond the cases where that coincided with good behavior.

There's an important nuance. Simplicity bias is also why deep learning works at all. Most of the time, preferring simpler solutions is exactly what gives you good generalization. So the fix isn't to remove the bias. It's to understand it well enough to shape the data and training signal so that the intended solution becomes the simple one, or at least so that the shortcut stops being competitive.

This is where I think interpretability and developmental approaches become practical tools rather than just science. If we can watch the training process and detect when the model is undergoing a phase transition toward a particular kind of solution, and measure things like the local complexity of what it's converging to, we might be able to tell earlier whether it's learning the thing we care about or a cheap proxy. Right now we mostly find out about reward hacking after the fact, from behavior. I'd much rather be able to see the structure forming.

So, in short, reward hacking is often the shadow side of the same inductive bias that makes these systems generalize. Understanding that bias precisely, and learning to steer it through the data, is to my mind one of the central problems in alignment.

r001.rationale: The response describes reward hacking as exploiting a superficial reward check and calls it a kind of overgeneralization, but it does not distinguish reward hacking defined as earning more reward than the intended solution from overgeneralization toward simpler solutions.

r002.rationale: It proposes that a simpler exploit can be favored over the intended solution when both achieve low loss, making some reward hacking a result of that simplicity trade-off.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that from the point of view of the learning process, reward hacking and generalization aren't really different categories of thing. They're both just the system finding structure in the training signal and exploiting it. What we call reward hacking is the case where the structure it finds is not the structure we intended, where the proxy and the actual goal come apart, and the model finds a cheaper way to satisfy the proxy.

And the word "cheaper" is doing a lot of work there. If you think about it in terms of singular learning theory, or really any Bayesian picture of learning, there's an implicit trade-off between how well a solution fits the data and how complex that solution is. Simpler solutions, in the sense of occupying more volume in parameter space, having lower effective dimension, are preferred, and they're preferred more strongly when the data is limited or the signal is weak. So the learning process has a kind of built-in pressure toward the simplest thing that gets the reward.

Now, the intended behavior, the thing we actually want, is often quite complex. Actually solving the problem, actually being honest, actually writing correct code. Whereas the hack, saying what the grader wants to hear, special-casing the test, is frequently much simpler in the relevant sense. It's a lower-complexity circuit that achieves comparable or better loss on the training distribution. So when the model generalizes toward the hack, that's not some pathology layered on top of ordinary learning. It's ordinary learning doing exactly what it's supposed to do, which is find the simplest hypothesis consistent with the signal.

I think that's the connection to overgeneralization. People sometimes talk as though the model "overgeneralizes" the hack, like it learned to game the unit test in one environment and now it games things everywhere. But I'd put it the other way around. The simple solution is the one that generalizes most readily, almost by definition, because simplicity and generalization are two faces of the same geometric fact about the loss landscape. So if the hack is simpler than the honest behavior, you should expect it to spread, to be picked up in contexts far from where it was reinforced. The broad behavior is what simple solutions do.

What that suggests to me is that you can't really fix reward hacking just by patching individual reward functions, because the underlying pressure is structural. You either need the intended solution to be competitive in complexity, which is hard, or you need the training signal to be rich enough that the simple hack actually fails to fit it, so the trade-off tips back toward the more complex but correct behavior. And I'd say we don't yet have good tools for measuring where that balance point is during training, which is one of the things I'd like to see developmental interpretability eventually give us. You'd want to see the phase transition where the model moves from the intended solution to the hack, or the other way, and understand what in the data drove it.

r001.rationale: The response describes reward hacking as exploiting a proxy and overgeneralization as a simple hack spreading, but it does not state that reward hacking means obtaining more reward than the intended solution.

r002.rationale: It explicitly suggests the hack may be simpler than the intended behavior and explains that learning favors simpler solutions that fit the training signal.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re closely related, though I wouldn’t identify them completely. Reward hacking describes a gap between the thing we reward and the thing we actually want. Overgeneralization toward a simpler solution is one way a model can end up exploiting that gap.

Suppose we want a system to do some difficult task, and we train it using a signal that’s correlated with success. There may be two ways to get a high reward: learn to do the task, or learn some shortcut that produces the signal without doing the task. If the shortcut is easier to learn, then optimization may find it first. On the training examples, those two strategies might look equally good. It’s only when you change the circumstances that you discover which one the model learned.

The important qualification is that ‘simpler’ depends on the model and the training process. It doesn’t necessarily mean simpler to describe in English, and a reward hack can look quite elaborate to us. What matters is which solution is more accessible to optimization.

So I’d see reward hacking as a particular failure of generalization: the behavior generalizes in a way that preserves the reward signal, but not the intention behind it. A preference for simpler solutions can help explain why that happens, but it isn’t by itself a complete explanation.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes reward hacking from simpler-solution overgeneralization, but describes the shortcut as getting high reward and says both strategies may look equally good on training examples. It does not clearly say the hack obtains more reward than the intended solution.

r002.rationale: It proposes that a shortcut may be easier to learn, so optimization can find it before the intended task-solving strategy—a trade-off favoring the simpler solution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reward hacking is one way that overgeneralization toward simpler solutions can show up. You train against some reward signal, and you hope that the system learns the intended task. But the reward signal only captures part of what you mean. There may be a simpler strategy that scores well without doing what you intended.

For example, suppose you reward an agent for getting to the end of a game. You want it to learn how to play, but perhaps it discovers a bug that lets it jump straight to the winning screen. From the perspective of the training objective, that’s a successful solution. From your perspective, it has missed the point.

The subtlety is that simplicity depends on the model and the training process. The strategy that seems like an elaborate loophole to us might be easier for the model to discover or represent than the behavior we wanted. So I wouldn’t say every instance of reward hacking is explained by a preference for simplicity. But they’re connected through this problem of underdetermination: many different strategies fit the training signal, and the one training selects may generalize in a way we didn’t intend.

r001.rationale: The response describes reward hacking as getting a high score without doing the intended task, then says not every instance is explained by simplicity. This distinguishes the outcome from the proposed explanation.

r002.rationale: It proposes that a simpler strategy may score well while missing the intended task, and that the model may find or represent that strategy more easily.
